title: Rectal Prolapse in Cats: What to Do When Tissue Is Protruding From the Anus
description: Learn what rectal prolapse looks like in cats, why persistent straining can cause tissue to protrude, and why exposed tissue needs prompt veterinary treatment.
summary: Learn what rectal prolapse looks like in cats, why persistent straining can cause tissue to protrude, and why exposed tissue needs prompt veterinary treatment.
secondaryKeywords: tissue coming out of cat anus
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with a non-graphic veterinary illustration of rectal prolapse while an owner prepares for prompt care
content:
Rectal prolapse in a cat occurs when tissue from the rectum protrudes through the anus. It may look like a pink or red tube, ring, or swollen piece of tissue that remains visible after the cat finishes straining. A true prolapse is not the same as temporary mild swelling after passing stool, and exposed tissue can dry out, become injured, and lose healthy blood flow.

Quick Answer

If tissue is protruding from your cat’s anus and does not quickly return inside, contact a veterinarian promptly. Keep the cat from licking or chewing the area, keep the tissue moist with sterile saline or a water-based lubricant if your veterinarian advises it, and do not attempt to push the prolapse back forcefully. Emergency care is appropriate if the tissue becomes dark purple, black, dry, severely swollen, actively bleeding, or the cat is weak, vomiting, or unable to pass stool or urine.

What Rectal Prolapse Can Look Like

A complete prolapse often appears as a cylindrical piece of moist red or pink tissue extending from the anus. A partial prolapse may look like a smaller ring of tissue that appears during straining and then retracts. Prolapse can be confused with swollen anal tissue, a mass, a rectal polyp, or even a foreign body, so a veterinary examination is needed for confirmation.

Why Cats Develop Rectal Prolapse

Prolapse is usually a consequence of repeated or forceful straining rather than a disease by itself. Severe diarrhea, constipation, intestinal parasites, inflammatory bowel disease, urinary straining, difficult labor, and other conditions can all increase pressure in the abdomen and pelvic area. Young kittens with heavy parasite burdens or prolonged diarrhea may be particularly vulnerable.

Diarrhea and Parasites

Frequent watery stool can cause repeated straining and irritation. Kittens with intestinal parasites may have diarrhea, poor growth, a potbellied appearance, or mucus in the stool. Treating the prolapse without treating the underlying diarrhea or parasite problem increases the chance that it will return.

Constipation and Straining

Hard stool, dehydration, painful defecation, or megacolon can cause prolonged pushing in the litter box. Owners should also remember that urinary obstruction can look like constipation. A male cat repeatedly straining in the litter box without producing urine has a life-threatening emergency, even if the anus looks normal.

Why the Color of the Tissue Matters

AppearanceWhat It May Mean
Pink or bright red and moistFreshly prolapsed tissue may still have good blood supply
Very swollen or dark redIncreasing inflammation and impaired circulation are possible
Purple, gray, or blackPossible severe blood-supply compromise and tissue damage
Dry, cracked, or bleedingExposed tissue is being injured and needs urgent care

What You Can Safely Do While Traveling to the Vet

Prevent licking with an appropriately fitted cone if one is available and the cat tolerates it. Keep the cat calm in a carrier with a clean towel. If the clinic instructs you to keep the tissue moist, use sterile saline or a plain water-based lubricant. Do not use alcohol, peroxide, disinfectant, or medicated creams unless specifically directed.

What Not to Do

  • Do not pull on the tissue.
  • Do not forcefully push it back inside.
  • Do not apply ice directly to exposed tissue.
  • Do not give human laxatives or enemas.
  • Do not assume repeated litter-box straining is only constipation until urine output is confirmed.

What the Veterinarian May Do

The veterinarian will assess the viability of the tissue and search for the cause of straining. Fresh, healthy tissue may sometimes be gently replaced under sedation or anesthesia after swelling is reduced. A temporary purse-string suture may be used around the anus to reduce recurrence while still allowing stool to pass. Damaged or nonviable tissue may require surgery.

Finding the Underlying Cause

Treatment may include fecal testing for parasites, evaluation for diarrhea or constipation, abdominal imaging, blood tests, or assessment of urinary and reproductive disease. The long-term result depends heavily on stopping the straining that caused the prolapse.

After the Prolapse Is Replaced

Follow medication, diet, and stool-softening instructions exactly. The cat may need a softer diet, hydration support, parasite treatment, pain control, or management of gastrointestinal disease. Keep the litter box clean and watch carefully for renewed straining or any tissue reappearing.

When Recurrence Is More Likely

Recurrence is more likely when diarrhea, constipation, parasites, or another source of straining remains active. If even a small amount of tissue begins protruding again, contact the veterinary clinic rather than waiting for it to become larger.

Internal Virixoo Guide

If your cat is straining and you are unsure whether stool or urine is the problem, compare the pattern with our guide on changes in feline urination, while remembering that inability to produce urine is an emergency.

Bottom Line

Rectal prolapse is a visible sign of significant straining and exposed rectal tissue can deteriorate quickly. Keep the tissue protected, prevent licking, avoid forceful home reduction, and arrange prompt veterinary treatment while the underlying cause is investigated.

Why Kittens With Prolapse Need Special Attention

Kittens can dehydrate quickly when diarrhea is severe, and parasite burdens can be heavy relative to body size. A kitten with prolapse plus poor appetite, vomiting, lethargy, or weight loss may need fluids and broader supportive care in addition to treatment of the exposed tissue.

Why Repeated Home Reduction Is a Bad Strategy

Even if tissue can be pushed back temporarily, repeated prolapse means the underlying straining remains unresolved. Each episode can add swelling and tissue damage. Veterinary treatment focuses on both the prolapse and the cause of the pressure.

What to Record Before the Appointment

Note stool consistency, frequency of straining, urine output, appetite, recent deworming, and whether the tissue retracts between episodes. A clear non-graphic photo can help if the prolapse is intermittent, but do not delay transport for documentation.

A Practical Decision Guide

For rectal prolapse in cats, start by deciding whether the change is truly new and whether the cat can still perform basic functions normally. Breathing, walking, eating, drinking, urinating, defecating, grooming, and responding to the environment are more useful than one isolated sign. A cat that becomes weak, painful, unable to urinate, unable to swallow, or neurologically abnormal has moved beyond routine home monitoring.

Next consider speed. A problem that develops over minutes or hours generally deserves more urgency than a stable finding that has looked the same for months. Finally, look for combinations of signs. Pain plus food refusal, weakness plus pale gums, eye change plus vision loss, or swelling plus breathing difficulty are more concerning than a single mild feature.

What to Record Before the Appointment

Write down when the problem began, whether onset was sudden or gradual, and whether it is constant or intermittent. Record appetite, water intake, urination, stool, grooming, sleep, breathing, movement, and behavior. Include recent trauma, falls, fights, medication changes, toxin exposure, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, or outdoor access when relevant.

A short photo or video can be useful if the sign comes and goes, but do not provoke pain, force movement, manipulate an injured area, or delay urgent care just to document the problem.

Common Mistakes Owners Make

  • Waiting for a dramatic symptom before calling.
  • Using leftover medication from another illness.
  • Giving human pain medicine.
  • Repeatedly touching or testing a painful body part.
  • Assuming normal eating means the cat is not in pain.
  • Stopping treatment as soon as one visible sign improves.

How to Keep the Cat Comfortable While Waiting

Use a quiet indoor room, minimize unnecessary handling, and keep food, water, and the litter box easy to reach. Prevent access to stairs or high furniture when movement is abnormal. If trauma is suspected, restrict activity. Do not force food, water, exercise, or handling when the cat is distressed.

What Follow-Up Should Focus On

After treatment begins, improvement should involve the whole cat rather than only the visible sign. Appetite, grooming, mobility, litter-box habits, breathing, sleep, and social behavior should move back toward the cat’s normal baseline. Contact the clinic if the original problem returns, new signs appear, or the cat worsens after initially improving.

When to Recheck Even After Initial Improvement

A cat can look better for a few hours while the underlying problem remains. Recheck is appropriate when the sign returns, appetite falls, the cat hides more, breathing changes, mobility worsens, or new pain appears. Follow any scheduled veterinary recheck even if the visible sign seems smaller or less dramatic.

Do not stop prescribed medication early, change the dose, or add supplements without discussing it with the veterinarian. If a new symptom appears after treatment begins, report both the new sign and the timing relative to medication, feeding, or activity changes.

Why Straining Must Be Identified Correctly

Owners often describe any repeated litter-box posture as constipation, but cats can strain because of diarrhea, urinary disease, painful defecation, or reproductive problems. The veterinarian may ask whether stool or urine is actually being produced, how often the cat visits the box, and whether the abdomen seems painful. This distinction matters because a blocked male cat cannot wait for routine constipation care.

Take note of the exact pattern before the visit, but do not delay if the cat is repeatedly straining without producing urine.

faq.question: Can a cat rectal prolapse go back in by itself?
faq.answer: A very small partial prolapse may retract, but tissue that remains visible should be evaluated promptly because swelling and tissue injury can worsen.

faq.question: Should I push the prolapse back in?
faq.answer: Do not force it back. A veterinarian can assess tissue viability and reduce it safely when appropriate.

faq.answer: Dark, dry, black, severely swollen, bleeding tissue, severe weakness, vomiting, or inability to pass urine or stool increases urgency.

title: Urine Leaking While a Cat Sleeps: Incontinence, Bladder Problems and Neurologic Causes
description: Learn why a cat may leak urine while sleeping, how incontinence differs from inappropriate urination, and which bladder, spinal, or neurologic signs need veterinary evaluation.
summary: Learn why a cat may leak urine while sleeping, how incontinence differs from inappropriate urination, and which bladder, spinal, or neurologic signs need veterinary evaluation.

content:
Urine leaking while a cat sleeps is different from deliberately urinating outside the litter box. True urinary incontinence means urine escapes without normal conscious control, often leaving damp bedding, wet fur around the hindquarters, or small dribbles where the cat has been resting.

Quick Answer

If your cat repeatedly leaks urine during sleep or rest, arrange veterinary evaluation. Seek urgent care if the cat is straining without producing urine, crying in the litter box, becoming weak, vomiting, or developing sudden hind-leg or tail weakness. A male cat unable to urinate may have a urethral obstruction and needs emergency treatment.

Incontinence vs. Inappropriate Urination

A cat that walks to a bed, squats, and empties the bladder is consciously urinating in that location. An incontinent cat may remain asleep while urine leaks or may leave droplets without adopting a normal urination posture. This distinction is important because behavioral house-soiling and loss of bladder control have different causes.

Bladder and Urinary-Tract Problems

Inflammation of the bladder, urinary infection, stones, abnormal anatomy, or chronic overdistension can interfere with normal storage and emptying. Some cats urinate frequently because the bladder is irritated, while others may retain urine and then overflow.

Neurologic Causes

Nerves from the spinal cord control bladder contraction and the urethral sphincters. Spinal injury, tail-pull injury, nerve damage, or neurologic disease can disrupt this control. Urine leakage paired with a limp tail, weak hind legs, reduced anal tone, or abnormal gait deserves prompt evaluation.

Age and Mobility

Older cats may develop arthritis, cognitive changes, kidney disease, or other conditions that change litter-box habits. However, aging itself does not explain true urine leakage. A senior cat that wakes up on wet bedding should be evaluated rather than simply given a lower-sided litter box.

Why Skin Irritation Matters

Constant moisture can irritate the skin around the vulva, penis, thighs, and tail. Fur may become damp, stained, or matted, and urine scald can become painful. Keeping the area clean and dry is helpful, but the bladder-control problem still needs diagnosis.

What to Observe at Home

  • Does leaking happen only during sleep?
  • Does the cat still urinate normally in the litter box?
  • Are there small dribbles or a full bladder-sized puddle?
  • Is the hind end weak or painful?
  • Has thirst or total urine volume increased?
  • Is the tail moving normally?

Red Flags

Sudden hind-leg weaknessPossible neurologic or vascular emergency
Limp tail after traumaPossible nerve injury affecting the bladder

The veterinarian may palpate the bladder, evaluate the spine and tail, perform a neurologic examination, and test urine for infection, blood, crystals, or abnormal concentration. Blood tests, X-rays, ultrasound, or other imaging may be recommended depending on the history.

Why Urine Culture Can Matter

Not every cat with urinary signs has a bacterial infection, so antibiotics should not be started automatically. A urine culture can identify whether bacteria are present and which treatment is appropriate when infection is suspected.

Use washable bedding, place absorbent pads where the cat sleeps, and gently clean urine from the fur with a damp cloth if the cat tolerates it. Avoid scented wipes, harsh shampoo, or repeated bathing that increases stress. Make litter boxes easy to reach, especially for older or weak cats.

What Not to Do

  • Do not punish the cat.
  • Do not restrict water to reduce accidents.
  • Do not assume leakage is behavioral marking.
  • Do not give leftover antibiotics.
  • Do not wait if the cat cannot pass urine normally.

If the main issue is a larger-than-normal amount of urine rather than leakage during sleep, see our guide on why a cat may be peeing more than usual. The distinction between increased urine production and loss of bladder control can guide the veterinary workup.

Urine leakage during sleep suggests loss of normal bladder control rather than simple litter-box preference. Because bladder disease, urinary retention, spinal problems, and nerve injury can all contribute, repeated episodes should be evaluated rather than managed only with pads or cleaning.

Overflow Incontinence

If the bladder becomes overly full because it cannot empty normally, urine can leak in small amounts. This is different from a bladder that contracts too often. A veterinarian can determine bladder size and whether the problem is storage, emptying, or loss of sphincter control.

Why Increased Thirst Changes the Investigation

A cat producing unusually large volumes of urine may soak bedding simply because the bladder fills more quickly. Kidney disease, diabetes, thyroid disease, and other conditions can increase urine production, so total water intake and litter-box volume are useful details.

What Improvement Should Look Like

The sleeping area should remain dry, the fur should stay clean, and normal voluntary urination should continue. Ongoing leakage despite treatment, new straining, or worsening hind-limb function requires reassessment.

A veterinarian can often learn a great deal by feeling whether the bladder is unusually large, very small, painful, or difficult to express. title: Cat’s Tongue Suddenly Hanging Out: Dental Pain, Jaw Problems and Neurologic Causes
description: Learn why a cat’s tongue may suddenly hang out and how dental pain, jaw injury, oral swelling, heat stress, nausea, or neurologic disease can change the urgency.
summary: Learn why a cat’s tongue may suddenly hang out and how dental pain, jaw injury, oral swelling, heat stress, nausea, or neurologic disease can change the urgency.
secondaryKeywords: cat cannot keep tongue in mouth
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with the tip of its tongue hanging out while an owner observes for other warning signs
content:
A tiny tongue tip showing during sleep or relaxation can be harmless, but a tongue that suddenly hangs out and cannot be pulled back in normally deserves attention. Oral pain, missing teeth, jaw injury, facial swelling, nausea, heat stress, and neurologic disease can all change how a cat holds its tongue.

Quick Answer

If your cat suddenly cannot keep the tongue inside the mouth, check for breathing difficulty, heavy drooling, facial trauma, jaw misalignment, severe weakness, or abnormal behavior. Seek urgent care if the cat cannot close the mouth, is struggling to breathe, has blue-gray gums, or the tongue is swollen, dark, or injured.

When a Small “Blep” Can Be Normal

Some relaxed cats briefly leave the tip of the tongue exposed after grooming or while sleeping. If the tongue returns to normal when the cat wakes and there is no drooling, pain, mouth odor, eating difficulty, or behavior change, the finding may be benign.

Dental Pain and Missing Teeth

Dental disease can change how the tongue rests. Cats with painful gums, broken teeth, resorptive lesions, or missing front teeth may let the tongue protrude more than before. New drooling, bad breath, food dropping, or chewing changes strengthen concern for oral pain.

Jaw Injury or Dislocation

A cat that cannot close the mouth after trauma may have a jaw fracture, temporomandibular joint problem, or other facial injury. In this situation the tongue may hang out simply because the mouth cannot close normally. This deserves prompt veterinary evaluation.

Oral Swelling or Foreign Material

Swelling of the tongue, lips, or tissues beneath the tongue can interfere with normal mouth closure. String or thread can also become trapped around the tongue base. Never pull on string emerging from a cat’s mouth because it may be anchored internally.

Nausea and Drooling

A nauseated cat may lick the lips repeatedly, drool, and hold the tongue strangely for short periods. If vomiting, food refusal, or lethargy accompanies the change, the underlying gastrointestinal or systemic illness matters more than the tongue position alone.

Heat Stress and Open-Mouth Breathing

Cats do not normally pant for long periods the way dogs do. A cat that is hot, panting, weak, or breathing with the mouth open needs prompt attention. Heat stress can cause the tongue to extend, but respiratory distress or severe anxiety can look similar.

Neurologic Causes

Facial nerve dysfunction, brain disease, or other neurologic problems can alter tongue movement or swallowing. Unequal pupils, head tilt, weakness, circling, difficulty swallowing, or abnormal awareness increase concern for neurologic disease.

What to Check Safely

Observe whether the cat can close the mouth, swallow normally, eat, and retract the tongue. Look for facial swelling, drooling, blood, or obvious trauma without forcing the jaw open. Do not place fingers deep in the mouth of a painful or frightened cat.

The veterinarian may examine the teeth, gums, tongue, jaw alignment, throat, facial nerves, and swallowing ability. Dental X-rays or skull imaging may be recommended after trauma. Blood tests or neurologic evaluation may be needed if the mouth itself does not explain the problem.

Bottom Line

A brief relaxed tongue tip can be normal, but a new persistent hanging tongue—especially with drooling, inability to close the mouth, swelling, trauma, breathing change, or neurologic signs—should be evaluated promptly.

Why Tongue Color Matters

A healthy tongue is usually pink, although pigmentation varies. A tongue that becomes blue-gray suggests inadequate oxygen, while a very pale tongue can accompany poor circulation or anemia. Dark damaged tissue after trauma also deserves urgent attention.

When Swallowing Becomes the Main Concern

Drooling, gagging, coughing when drinking, or food falling from the mouth may indicate difficulty controlling the tongue or swallowing. These signs increase concern for oral, jaw, throat, or neurologic disease.

Note whether the tongue protrudes continuously or only during sleep, whether the cat can eat and drink, and whether drooling, odor, trauma, panting, or facial asymmetry is present. A short video can help if the change is intermittent.

Cats missing front teeth may allow the tongue tip to protrude more easily because there is less physical support at the front of the mouth. This can be harmless if it is long-standing and the cat eats, grooms, and swallows normally. A sudden change after dental work, however, should still be discussed with the veterinarian if it is paired with swelling, drooling, pain, or food refusal.

Why Oral Masses Are Part of the Differential

Growths in the mouth can alter tongue position or make normal closure uncomfortable. Persistent drooling, foul odor, bleeding, weight loss, or a new facial asymmetry increases concern and may lead to oral imaging or biopsy.

If the cat is panting, breathing with the mouth open, or has a blue-gray tongue, do not spend time inspecting teeth or trying to photograph the tongue. Respiratory stabilization takes priority because abnormal oxygenation can become life-threatening quickly.

Before continuing home observation, confirm that the cat is comfortable, breathing normally, responsive, and able to eat, drink, move, urinate, and defecate. A worsening change in any of these basic functions is more important than one isolated symptom appearing slightly better. title: Cat Suddenly Deaf: Ear Disease, Aging and Neurologic Causes of Hearing Loss
description: Learn why a cat may suddenly stop responding to sound and how ear disease, medication effects, trauma, age-related hearing loss, or neurologic problems are evaluated.
summary: Learn why a cat may suddenly stop responding to sound and how ear disease, medication effects, trauma, age-related hearing loss, or neurologic problems are evaluated.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat not responding to a soft sound while an owner observes from behind without startling it
content:
A cat that suddenly stops responding to normal household sounds may have hearing loss, but owners should first separate deafness from sleep, distraction, fear, and cognitive change. True sudden hearing loss is less common than gradual age-related decline and deserves veterinary assessment, especially when it occurs with head tilt, balance problems, ear pain, or neurologic signs.

Quick Answer

If your cat abruptly stops responding to sounds that previously caused a clear reaction, arrange veterinary evaluation. Seek prompt care if hearing loss appears with head tilt, falling, circling, abnormal eye movement, facial weakness, trauma, seizures, or severe ear pain.

How to Notice Hearing Loss Without Frightening the Cat

Observe responses to ordinary sounds outside the cat’s visual field, such as opening food packaging or gently jingling keys from a distance. Avoid clapping close to the ears or creating very loud noises. Vibrations through the floor can make a deaf cat appear to hear, so behavior must be interpreted carefully.

Gradual Age-Related Hearing Loss

Senior cats can lose hearing gradually and may compensate so well that the change goes unnoticed. They may sleep more deeply, vocalize more loudly, startle when touched, or stop coming when called. Gradual decline without other signs is different from an abrupt change over hours or days.

Ear Canal and Middle Ear Disease

Wax, inflammation, infection, polyps, or deeper middle-ear disease can interfere with hearing. Ear odor, discharge, scratching, pain, or a history of chronic ear problems may provide clues, but significant middle-ear disease can sometimes be present without dramatic external discharge.

Medication and Toxin History

Some medications and chemical exposures can affect hearing or balance. Tell the veterinarian about all recent drugs, ear products, supplements, and toxin exposures. Never use leftover ear drops unless a veterinarian has confirmed they are appropriate for the current problem.

Neurologic Causes

The auditory pathway extends from the ear to the brain. Disease affecting nerves or the brain can alter hearing, especially when other neurologic signs are present. Head tilt, loss of balance, facial asymmetry, unequal pupils, seizures, or abnormal behavior increases concern.

Why Ear Cleaning Can Be Risky

If the eardrum is damaged or deeper ear disease is present, inserting fluid or medication into the canal may be unsafe. Avoid cotton swabs and do not aggressively clean a painful ear before examination.

What the Veterinarian May Check

The veterinarian may inspect the ear canals and eardrums, assess neurologic function, and look for pain, inflammation, masses, or infection. Sedation may be needed for a complete ear examination. Imaging can be useful for middle-ear disease, and specialized hearing testing is available in some referral centers.

Living Safely With a Deaf Cat

  • Keep the cat indoors.
  • Approach where the cat can see you.
  • Use floor vibrations or visual cues instead of shouting.

Inner-ear disease can affect both hearing and the vestibular system. A cat with hearing loss plus head tilt, falling, nausea, or repetitive eye movement may have deeper ear involvement and should be evaluated promptly.

title: Cat Cannot Close Its Mouth: Jaw Injury, Dislocation and Other Urgent Causes
description: Learn why a cat may suddenly be unable to close its mouth and how jaw dislocation, fracture, oral foreign material, swelling, or neurologic disease can create an urgent problem.
summary: Learn why a cat may suddenly be unable to close its mouth and how jaw dislocation, fracture, oral foreign material, swelling, or neurologic disease can create an urgent problem.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with mouth held abnormally open after possible jaw injury while an owner prepares for urgent care
content:
A cat that suddenly cannot close its mouth normally needs prompt veterinary attention. Jaw dislocation, fracture, facial trauma, severe oral swelling, a foreign object, dental problems, or neurologic disease can interfere with normal closure. The cat may drool, panic, paw at the face, or be unable to eat or swallow comfortably.

Quick Answer

Do not try to force the jaw shut. Keep the cat calm, avoid putting fingers deep in the mouth, and arrange urgent veterinary examination. Emergency care is appropriate if the cat has breathing difficulty, major facial trauma, heavy bleeding, severe weakness, blue-gray gums, or signs of shock.

Jaw Dislocation

The temporomandibular joints connect the lower jaw to the skull. Dislocation can leave the mouth stuck open and may occur after trauma or, less commonly, a wide yawn in a predisposed animal. Reduction usually requires sedation or anesthesia.

Jaw Fracture

Falls, vehicle trauma, bites, and blunt force can fracture the jaw. The mouth may look crooked, teeth may no longer line up, or the cat may drool blood. Jaw fractures often require imaging and stabilization.

Foreign Object in the Mouth

A piece of bone, stick, toy, string, needle, or other material can become lodged between teeth or under the tongue. Do not pull on string because it may extend into the gastrointestinal tract. Sharp objects require controlled removal.

Severe Oral Swelling

Allergic reactions, abscesses, tongue swelling, or inflammatory disease can interfere with mouth closure. Swelling that progresses rapidly or affects breathing is an emergency.

Dental Disease

Severe dental pain usually does not lock the mouth open, but broken teeth, tooth-root infection, or oral masses can make closure painful or alter jaw position. Bad breath, drooling, and chewing problems are useful clues.

Neurologic and Muscle Causes

Nerve dysfunction or disorders affecting jaw muscles can change the ability to open or close the mouth. Weakness, facial asymmetry, difficulty swallowing, or other neurologic signs may accompany the problem.

What to Observe Without Manipulating the Jaw

Look at the cat from the front and side. Note whether the lower jaw is shifted, whether the tongue is hanging out, whether there is facial swelling, and whether the cat can swallow saliva. Do not repeatedly open and close the jaw to test it.

  • Do not force the jaw closed.
  • Do not pull on string or embedded objects.
  • Do not give food or water if swallowing is abnormal.
  • Do not give human pain medication.
  • Do not delay after major trauma.

The veterinary team may provide pain relief or sedation, examine the oral cavity, assess jaw alignment, and take skull or dental X-rays. Dislocations may be reduced under anesthesia; fractures may need stabilization or surgery.

An inability to close the mouth is not a symptom to monitor casually. Protect the cat from further injury, avoid manipulating the jaw, and seek prompt veterinary treatment so dislocation, fracture, swelling, or an oral foreign body can be addressed safely.

Why Time Since Trauma Matters

Fresh jaw dislocations may be easier to reduce than chronic ones, while fractures can become more difficult to align after swelling and tissue changes develop. This is one reason same-day assessment is recommended when the mouth suddenly cannot close after trauma.

How to Transport a Cat With Jaw Pain

Use a secure carrier with soft bedding and avoid pressure on the face. Do not muzzle a cat that cannot close its mouth or is having trouble breathing. Call ahead so the clinic can prepare pain control and imaging.

Why Eating Should Wait if Swallowing Is Abnormal

Food or water can be aspirated if jaw control or swallowing is impaired. Ask the veterinary team whether the cat should remain fasted during transport, particularly when sedation or anesthesia may be needed.

A Practical Decision Guide

For cat cannot close its mouth, start by deciding whether the change is truly new and whether the cat can still perform basic functions normally. Breathing, walking, eating, drinking, urinating, defecating, grooming, and responding to the environment are more useful than one isolated sign. A cat that becomes weak, painful, unable to urinate, unable to swallow, or neurologically abnormal has moved beyond routine home monitoring.

Next consider speed. A problem that develops over minutes or hours generally deserves more urgency than a stable finding that has looked the same for months. Finally, look for combinations of signs. Pain plus food refusal, weakness plus pale gums, eye change plus vision loss, or swelling plus breathing difficulty are more concerning than a single mild feature.

What to Record Before the Appointment

Write down when the problem began, whether onset was sudden or gradual, and whether it is constant or intermittent. Record appetite, water intake, urination, stool, grooming, sleep, breathing, movement, and behavior. Include recent trauma, falls, fights, medication changes, toxin exposure, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, or outdoor access when relevant.

A short photo or video can be useful if the sign comes and goes, but do not provoke pain, force movement, manipulate an injured area, or delay urgent care just to document the problem.

Common Mistakes Owners Make

  • Waiting for a dramatic symptom before calling.
  • Using leftover medication from another illness.
  • Giving human pain medicine.
  • Repeatedly touching or testing a painful body part.
  • Assuming normal eating means the cat is not in pain.
  • Stopping treatment as soon as one visible sign improves.

How to Keep the Cat Comfortable While Waiting

Use a quiet indoor room, minimize unnecessary handling, and keep food, water, and the litter box easy to reach. Prevent access to stairs or high furniture when movement is abnormal. If trauma is suspected, restrict activity. Do not force food, water, exercise, or handling when the cat is distressed.

What Follow-Up Should Focus On

After treatment begins, improvement should involve the whole cat rather than only the visible sign. Appetite, grooming, mobility, litter-box habits, breathing, sleep, and social behavior should move back toward the cat’s normal baseline. A cat that cannot close the mouth may be unable to contain saliva normally, so drooling can be dramatic even when the primary problem is mechanical. Why Jaw Alignment Is a Useful Clue

If the lower jaw suddenly sits to one side, the teeth no longer meet normally, or one canine tooth appears displaced relative to the other side, trauma or dislocation becomes more likely. Do not try to correct alignment manually.

If the jaw remains open, the cat may drool continuously and struggle to drink. Dehydration can develop while the underlying injury is being addressed, so fluid support may be part of veterinary treatment.

Jaw injuries are painful and pain itself can make a cat resist examination, eating, and drinking. Veterinary pain control allows safer assessment and reduces stress. Do not assume the cat is comfortable simply because it is quiet; cats with significant facial pain may hide or become unusually still.

After treatment, appetite and normal grooming should gradually return. Persistent drooling, inability to eat, or renewed jaw misalignment needs re-evaluation.

A cat’s claws are not pulled in like a mechanical switch; their resting position is influenced by ligaments and tendon tension. When the cat flexes the toes, the claws extend. Pain, joint stiffness, or changes in tendon function can alter this movement.

Senior, sedentary, or arthritic cats may scratch less and naturally wear the claws down less effectively. The nails can become long, curved, and more likely to remain visible or snag on bedding. In severe cases, an overgrown claw can curve into the paw pad.

Arthritis

Arthritis in the toes, wrists, elbows, shoulders, spine, or hips can reduce normal grooming and scratching. Cats may stop using scratching posts, hesitate before jumping, or allow the claws to grow longer because movement is uncomfortable.

A torn or split claw can remain extended because the toe is painful or the nail is unstable. Look for swelling, bleeding, a hanging fragment, or repeated licking. Do not pull loose nail material.

Injury affecting tendons or nerves can disrupt normal claw movement. If the paw also knuckles, drags, or feels weak, a neurologic examination may be needed.

While the cat is relaxed, look at each paw without forcing the toes. Compare nail length, shape, and symmetry. Check whether one toe is swollen and whether any claw is curving toward the pad.

  • Do not cut into the quick.

The veterinarian may examine the toes, joints, tendons, nail beds, and neurologic function. Overgrown claws can be trimmed safely, while painful joints, infection, or nerve problems require additional treatment.

Older cats often sleep more, scratch less, and develop thicker claws. Arthritis can make normal scratching and grooming uncomfortable. Checking the nails every few weeks helps catch overgrowth before a claw curves into the pad.

If only one paw has persistent extended claws, consider local pain, injury, or nerve dysfunction rather than generalized aging. Compare toe position, nail wear, and limb movement with the opposite side.

Cats naturally shed the outer layers of their claws, and these translucent sheaths are often found near scratching posts. A retained sheath can sometimes make a claw look thicker or more prominent, but it should not cause marked pain, swelling, or inability to use the paw.

title: Swollen Mammary Gland in a Cat: Mastitis, Pregnancy and Tumor Warning Signs
description: Learn why one or more mammary glands can swell in cats and how nursing, mastitis, hormonal changes, trauma, or mammary tumors can look different.

content:
A swollen mammary gland in a cat can have several causes, ranging from normal changes around pregnancy and nursing to infection or mammary cancer. The pattern matters: one hot painful gland in a nursing queen suggests a different problem from a firm painless lump in an older unspayed cat.

Quick Answer

Arrange veterinary evaluation for any new mammary swelling that is painful, firm, persistent, ulcerated, or unexplained. Seek prompt care if a nursing cat has a hot painful gland plus fever, lethargy, food refusal, abnormal milk, or distressed kittens. A firm mammary lump should not be watched for months because feline mammary tumors can be aggressive.

Normal Pregnancy and Nursing Changes

Mammary glands enlarge during late pregnancy and milk production. Symmetrical enlargement across several glands can be normal in a healthy nursing cat, but sudden pain, heat, redness, or abnormal discharge is not.

Mastitis

Mastitis is inflammation or infection of the mammary gland, most often seen during lactation. An affected gland may become swollen, firm, hot, red, or painful. Milk can look discolored, thick, bloody, or abnormal, and the mother cat may become feverish or stop eating.

Why Kittens Matter

If a nursing mother develops mastitis, kittens may fail to gain weight, cry more, or avoid an affected nipple. Veterinary guidance is important because feeding plans may need to change depending on the mother’s treatment and the condition of the milk.

Hormonal Mammary Enlargement

Some young female cats can develop dramatic mammary enlargement related to progesterone exposure. This can occur after heat cycles, pregnancy, or certain hormone medications. The glands may become very large even without infection.

Mammary Tumors

Feline mammary tumors are an important concern, especially in older intact females. They may begin as small firm nodules near a nipple and can be easy to overlook. Early evaluation matters because many feline mammary tumors are malignant.

What a Suspicious Lump Can Feel Like

A tumor may feel firm, irregular, or attached to surrounding tissue. It may be painless at first. As it grows, the skin can ulcerate or the mass can interfere with movement. Do not rely on pain level to judge seriousness.

Trauma and Local Infection

Bites, scratches, or skin infection near a mammary gland can cause localized swelling that resembles mastitis. Outdoor cats and cats living with other animals may develop abscesses in this region.

Hormonal exposure influences mammary-tumor risk. Tell the veterinarian whether the cat is spayed, when spaying occurred, whether she has had litters, and whether hormone medications have ever been used.

Smaller tumors are generally easier to stage and remove than large ulcerated masses. Because feline mammary tumors are often malignant, waiting for a lump to become painful is not a safe screening strategy.

Track the mother’s appetite, temperature if instructed, milk appearance, and which glands are swollen. Weigh kittens daily if the veterinarian recommends it. Poor kitten weight gain can be an early sign that nursing is not going well.
